---
title: "How these systems actually work: from the eGFR on a chemistry panel to the next word"
subtitle: "AIM-1 · AIM-2 · about 75 minutes"
---

::: {.callout-note title="What you'll learn"}
By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

1. Explain, using eGFR as the worked example, what it means for a formula to be
   *learned from data* rather than derived, and name its predictors, its
   response, and the population it was learned from.
2. Tell supervised from unsupervised learning by asking what the training data
   contains, and classification from regression by asking what the model
   emits.
3. Say why a model's performance on data it has already seen tells you nothing
   useful, and why separating training from test data is the non-negotiable
   minimum.
4. Describe in plain words what a language model computes at each step, and
   use that description to explain a fabricated citation or a confident wrong
   answer as a property of the mechanism rather than a bug.
5. Name two structural limits of the context window, that it is a shared budget
   and that material buried in the middle is attended to less reliably, and say
   what each one changes about how you will prompt.
:::

**Time.** About 22 minutes of reading, 27 minutes of watching, 20 minutes of
doing, and 6 minutes for the check and the standing question. No math and no
coding are assumed; the only equation in the chapter is one you already use.
You need a browser and your institutional ChatGPT Edu or Microsoft Copilot
account. Nothing installs, and nothing asks you for a phone number.

## The number nobody measured

Pre-operative clinic, your surgery sub-internship. A 62-year-old woman is being
worked up for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Her basic metabolic panel is
back, and one line is flagged.

::: {.lab-report}
<div class="hdr">Basic metabolic panel · collected 07:12</div>
<table>
<tr><td>Sodium</td><td>139</td><td></td><td>136–145 mmol/L</td></tr>
<tr><td>Potassium</td><td>4.1</td><td></td><td>3.5–5.1 mmol/L</td></tr>
<tr><td>Creatinine</td><td>1.10</td><td></td><td>0.50–1.10 mg/dL</td></tr>
<tr><td>eGFR (CKD-EPI 2021)</td><td>57</td><td class="flag">L</td><td>&gt;60 mL/min/1.73 m²</td></tr>
</table>
<div class="fine">Illustrative panel for this chapter; not a real patient's result.</div>
:::

The attending asks whether her kidneys are all right for the contrast CT the
surgeon wants. You answer the way everyone answers: "eGFR 57, stage 3a, mildly
reduced, probably fine with hydration." The attending nods. That is the whole
conversation, and it is a conversation you will have several hundred times in
intern year.

Now the question this chapter hangs on. Nobody measured her glomerular
filtration rate. Measuring it means infusing a marker the kidney filters and
does nothing else with, such as inulin or iohexol, and timing how fast it
clears; it takes hours and it is done almost exclusively in research studies.
The 57 on the panel was *computed* from three things the lab did have: her
creatinine, her age, and her sex. Something turned those three numbers into a
kidney function, and you trusted it enough to clear her for contrast.

Where did that formula come from? Not from physiology. Nobody derived it from
first principles about nephrons. It was **learned from data**: from a few
thousand people who did have their GFR measured, and whose creatinine, age, and
sex were fed to a computer with the instruction to find the formula that best
predicted the measured number. The eGFR is a model. It is the model you already
trust most, and you have never once asked what it was trained on.

Hold on to the patient. She weighs 45 kilograms and has lost a good deal of
muscle over a year of intermittent illness. We will come back to her.

## Why this matters

In three months you will be handed a dozen of these. A sepsis alert that fires
in the EHR. A risk score that decides who gets a phone call after discharge. A
scribe that drafts your note. A chatbot that answers a dosing question at 2
a.m. Every one of them is the same kind of object as the eGFR: a formula
learned from some population, applied to your patient, with failures that
follow from how it was built. The skill this chapter teaches is not building
these things. It is looking at one and predicting how it will fail, in the
thirty seconds before you act on it.

The second half of the chapter does this for the language model specifically,
because its failure mode is the strangest and the most fluent. It will hand
you a citation that does not exist, formatted perfectly, and it will do so for
a reason that follows directly from what it computes. Once you can say that
reason out loud, "it hallucinates" stops being a shrug and becomes a
prediction about when to check.

## The idea

### A formula learned from data

The eGFR your lab reports almost certainly uses the CKD-EPI 2021 equation. Here
is how it was made. Investigators pooled ten studies in which 8,254 people had
their GFR measured directly with a filtration marker, and also had a
standardized creatinine, an age, and a sex on record. They then fit an
equation that predicts the measured GFR from those three inputs as closely as
possible across all 8,254 people; "fit" means a computer tried coefficients
until the predictions were as close to the measured values as they could get. They tested it on a
separate set of 4,050 people from twelve other studies, whose measured GFR the
equation had never seen [@pmid:34554658].

That paragraph contains every term you need for the rest of the course, so
here they are, named:

- **Predictors** are the inputs: creatinine, age, sex. The literature also
  calls them features or variables.
- The **response** is the thing being predicted: measured GFR. Also called the
  label, the outcome, or the truth.
- The **training set** is the 8,254 people whose predictors and response were
  used to fit the equation. The **test set** is the 4,050 the equation was
  checked on afterwards.
- The **model** is the equation itself, once fit: `eGFR = f(creatinine, age, sex)`.
  The *f* is whatever shape the fitting procedure settled on; for CKD-EPI it
  is a handful of exponents and coefficients, and for the systems later in
  this chapter it is billions of numbers, but the role is the same.

@fig-egfr-proxy shows what that model actually connects. The thing you want
to know is on the right. The thing the lab can measure is on the left. The
equation is the bridge, and the bridge was built from a specific set of
people.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-egfr-proxy
%%| fig-alt: "Flowchart. Three inputs the lab has, serum creatinine, age, and sex, feed an equation learned from 8,254 people with measured GFR, which outputs the eGFR on the panel. A dotted arrow shows the eGFR standing in for measured GFR, which is never done in routine care. A grey box, muscle mass, diet, and drugs that block secretion, feeds creatinine without touching measured GFR."
%%| fig-cap: "What the eGFR equation takes in and what it stands for. The equation was learned from 8,254 people with measured GFR; it is a bridge from what a lab can measure to what a clinician wants to know, and everything that moves creatinine without moving GFR (grey) crosses the bridge undetected. Redrawn from the description of the CKD-EPI 2021 development in Inker et al. (2021)."
flowchart LR
  subgraph IN["What the lab has"]
    direction TB
    cr[Serum creatinine]
    age[Age]
    sex[Sex]
  end
  eq["eGFR = f(creatinine, age, sex)<br/>learned from 8,254 people<br/>whose GFR was measured"]
  out["eGFR<br/>(a number on your panel)"]
  truth["Measured GFR<br/>(iohexol or iothalamate clearance;<br/>never done in routine care)"]
  cr --> eq
  age --> eq
  sex --> eq
  eq --> out
  out -. "stands in for" .-> truth
  muscle["Muscle mass · diet ·<br/>drugs that block secretion"]:::grey -.-> cr
  classDef grey fill:#eee,stroke:#999,color:#555
```

Three things follow from "learned from data", and each one is a question you
can ask of any model.

**The truth column existed.** For every one of the 8,254 people, someone had
gone to the trouble of measuring the real GFR. That is what makes this
**supervised learning**: the training data contains the answer, and the model
learns to reproduce it. **Unsupervised learning** is what you do when there is
no answer column, only patterns to find, such as sorting 10,000 tumor
expression profiles into clusters without being told which are which. The test
is simple: does the training data contain the thing you want predicted?

**The model emits a number.** eGFR is a quantity, so this is **regression**:
the output is a value on a scale. If the same inputs were used to output "CKD:
yes or no", that would be **classification**: the output is a category. Most
clinical prediction tools are one or the other, and the distinction decides
how you judge them. A regression is wrong by an amount; a classification is
wrong by a *kind*, a miss or a false alarm, and those two kinds cost different
people different things.

**The model is exactly as good as the people it was fit to.** The 8,254 were
mostly participants in kidney research studies, 31.5 percent of them Black,
none of them children, none of them your patient. Every population outside
that set is an extrapolation, and the history of the equation is a history of
finding out where the extrapolation broke.

### The history of one equation is the history of its training set

| Equation | Year | Learned from | Tested on | What broke, and where |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MDRD | 1999 | 1,628 patients with chronic kidney disease, of whom 1,070 were the training sample | The remaining 558 | Fit to people with reduced GFR; systematically underestimated GFR at higher values, so healthy people were labeled as diseased [@pmid:10075613; @pmid:19414839] |
| CKD-EPI | 2009 | 8,254 participants in 10 studies | 3,896 in 16 studies | More accurate at higher GFR, but carried a coefficient for Black race that the 2021 validation showed overestimated measured GFR in Black adults by a median of 3.7 mL/min/1.73 m² [@pmid:19414839; @pmid:34554658] |
| CKD-EPI 2021 | 2021 | 8,254 participants in 10 studies, refit without race | 4,050 in 12 studies | Now recommended for all US laboratories; the refit without race still underestimates in Black adults and overestimates in non-Black adults by a few mL/min, and a cystatin C version is more accurate [@pmid:34554658; @pmid:34563581] |

: Three generations of the eGFR equation, rebuilt from the numbers in the papers. Each one is a formula learned from a population, and each one's known failure lives outside that population. {#tbl-egfr-history}

Read the last column as a pattern rather than as nephrology. Every row says
the same thing: *the model was fit to these people, and here is what happened
to those people.* The bias and equity chapter takes up why the race coefficient
was there in the first place and who paid for it. For this chapter the point
is narrower and it generalizes: the training population is a property of the
model, as much as the equation is, and you cannot judge the one without
knowing the other.

### The loop, in general

Every model in this course, from the eGFR to the chatbot, was built by the
same loop, drawn once in @fig-loop.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-loop
%%| fig-alt: "Flowchart. Raw material such as labs, images, notes, or text becomes predictors; the truth for each case, such as measured GFR, sepsis yes or no, or the next word, joins them in a learning step that finds a function f so that truth is approximately f of predictors; the result is a model, and a new case with unknown truth goes through the model to produce a prediction."
%%| fig-cap: "The loop every learned model comes from. Turn the raw material into predictors, collect the truth for each case, learn a function that predicts truth from predictors, then apply it to a case whose truth you do not have. The eGFR, a sepsis alert, and a language model differ only in what fills the boxes."
flowchart LR
  raw[Raw material:<br/>labs, images, notes, text] --> pred[Predictors]
  truth[Truth for each case:<br/>measured GFR, sepsis yes/no,<br/>the next word] --> learn
  pred --> learn["Learn: find f so that<br/>truth ≈ f(predictors)"]
  learn --> model["Model: response = f(predictors)"]
  new[New case, truth unknown] --> model --> ans[Prediction]
```

You now have two questions that classify any model in about ten seconds, and
they are the ones the Check asks you to apply:

| Question | If yes | If no |
|---|---|---|
| Does the training data contain the answer? | Supervised | Unsupervised |
| Does the model emit a category? | Classification | Regression (a number) |

: Two questions that sort any model. {#tbl-two-questions}

### Why performance on data it has seen tells you nothing

Here is the trap the eGFR investigators avoided, and the one every vendor
slide invites you into. If you fit a formula to 8,254 people and then report
how well it predicts GFR *in those same 8,254 people*, you have measured how
well the formula memorized them, not how well it will work on the next
patient. A sufficiently flexible model can fit its training data perfectly and
be useless. Its performance on data it has already seen is not evidence; it is
a description of the fitting procedure.

![Every one of these fits the same data. The one on the bottom right fits it best. xkcd 2048, *Curve-Fitting*, by Randall Munroe, [CC BY-NC 2.5](https://xkcd.com/license.html) (non-commercial use only).](../images/curve_fitting.png){#fig-xkcd-curve .comic fig-alt="xkcd comic: a grid of twelve scatterplots of the same data, each with a different fitted curve and a caption, from a straight line labeled linear, through quadratic and logarithmic, to a wildly wiggling curve labeled 'connecting lines' with the caption 'I clicked a button and this came out', and one labeled 'house of cards' that fits every point."}

That is why the train/test separation is the non-negotiable minimum. You fit
on one set of cases and you report performance on a *different* set the model
never saw. The 4,050-person validation set in the eGFR paper is that second
set. When a claim about a model gives you one number and does not say which
set it came from, you do not yet have a number.

Two ways to be wrong give the idea its vocabulary. A model that is **too
simple** cannot capture the real relationship no matter how much data it sees;
the straight line through a curve. Statisticians call that error *bias*, in
a technical sense unrelated to the social one. A model that is **too
flexible** captures the noise in its particular training set along with the
signal, so it fits those cases beautifully and the next case badly; the wiggle
through every point. That error is *variance*. You will see both in the
exercise, in about eight minutes, on your own screen, and the third sentence
you write there is the one that transfers to every performance claim you are
ever shown.

The clinical version of the same failure is **dataset shift**: the world the
model meets in deployment differs from the world in its training set, so
performance measured at development does not carry over [@pmid:34260843]. A
sepsis model built by one EHR vendor and running in hundreds of US hospitals
was externally validated at one academic center on 38,455 hospitalizations. It
had an area under the curve of 0.63, on a scale where 0.5 is a coin flip and
1.0 is perfect discrimination, missed 67 percent of patients with sepsis, and
alerted on 18 percent of all admissions [@pmid:34152373]. Nobody
had lied about the development performance. It simply had not been measured on
patients like those.

::: {.callout-important title="The one sentence"}
A model's performance on the population it was built from is the optimistic
number. Ask what it was trained on, and ask what it was tested on, and if
those are the same set you have learned nothing yet.
:::

### From tables to words

Everything so far had a table: one row per patient, one column per predictor,
one column of truth. A language model is the same loop with a different table,
and seeing that is the whole trick.

Take any sentence from the internet: *the patient was started on empiric*.
Chop it into **tokens**, which are words or pieces of words; "empiric" might
be one token and "vancomycin" three. Now the predictors are the tokens so far,
and the truth is the very next token. You do not need anyone to label
anything, because the next word is already sitting there in the text. Every
sentence ever written becomes a training case for free, which is why these
models could be trained on a very large fraction of the written internet.

To make tokens usable by the loop, each one is turned into a list of numbers,
called an **embedding**, chosen so that tokens used in similar contexts get
similar numbers. "Vancomycin" ends up near "linezolid" and far from
"Tuesday". That is the "translate data into predictors" box of @fig-loop, done
for words.

The model is then trained to do one thing: given the tokens so far, produce a
probability for every possible next token. Then a token is drawn from that
distribution, appended, and the process runs again. A paragraph of fluent
medical prose is a few hundred repetitions of *predict the next token, pick
one, repeat*. Your phone's keyboard does this with a vocabulary of a few
thousand words and a look-back of two or three; these models do it with a
vocabulary of roughly a hundred thousand tokens, a look-back of many thousands,
and a function *f* with hundreds of billions of numbers in it. The video you
will watch shows what that function looks like from the inside. What matters
here is what it does not contain.

There is a second training stage, and it explains the tone. After the
next-token training, people are paid to compare pairs of answers and say which
one they prefer, and the model is tuned toward the preferred kind. The
literature calls this reinforcement learning from human feedback. It is what
turns a text-completer into an assistant that answers your question, in
paragraphs, politely. It also means the model has been optimized for answers
people *rate well*, which is not the same as answers that are true, and in
practice it tends to reward confidence and completeness, because a hedged,
incomplete answer loses those comparisons. A general review for clinicians of how these
chatbots are built, and of the mixed results so far, is a good next read
[@pmid:37460753].

Now the sentence the chapter was built to deliver:

::: {.callout-important title="Nothing in this mechanism checks whether a claim is true"}
At no step does the model look anything up, consult a database, or compare a
statement to the world. It produces the most plausible next token, given the
tokens so far and given what people rated well. A real citation and a
fabricated one are both plausible continuations of "the original paper was".
The model is not lying, and it is not malfunctioning. It is doing exactly what
it was built to do, and the thing it was built to do has no truth step in it.
:::

Here is what that looks like when it reaches you. The exchange below is
illustrative, constructed for this chapter; the scoring system, the point
values it gives, and the reference are the kind of thing a model produces, not
a transcript.

::: {.chat}
<div class="user">What are the exact point values and cutoffs for the HEART score, and what is the original publication?</div>
<div class="bot">The HEART score assigns 0–2 points each for History, ECG, Age, Risk factors, and Troponin, for a total of 0–10. Patients scoring 0–3 are low risk (about 1.7% risk of a major adverse cardiac event at 6 weeks) and can be discharged; 4–6 is intermediate (about 12–17%); 7–10 is high risk (about 50–65%) and warrants early invasive management.<br/><br/>Original publication: Backus BE, Six AJ, Kelder JC, et al. "A prospective validation of the HEART score for chest pain patients at the emergency department." <em>Int J Cardiol.</em> 2013;168(3):2153–2158.</div>
<div class="fine">Illustrative exchange, constructed for this chapter. Do not use it as a source for the HEART score.</div>
:::

Read it as a clinician and it is fine. Read it as a student of the mechanism
and every clause is a plausible continuation. The structure is right. The
names are real people who have written about this score. The journal exists.
Whether the *original* publication is the one named, whether the percentages
are from that paper or a later one or nowhere, whether the cutoffs match what
MDCalc shows, is not something the model checked, because checking is not a
step. You will find out in the exercise; the original description of the score
is in fact in a different journal and year [@pmid:18665203], and that is
precisely the kind of detail that a fluent continuation gets *almost* right.

::: {.callout-note title="What this does and does not mean"}
It does not mean the answer is usually wrong. On common questions these models
are right most of the time, because the most plausible continuation of a
well-documented fact is the fact. It means the *error rate is not zero and the
tone does not change when it is wrong.* A fabricated citation reads exactly
like a real one. That is the justified part of the fear; the outdated part is
the belief that the tools are unreliable for everything. The critical
appraisal chapter measures the rates. This chapter explains why there is a
rate at all.
:::

### The context window

One more structural fact, because it changes how you will type. Everything the
model can see at once, your question, anything you pasted, the conversation so
far, and its own reply as it writes it, has to fit inside a fixed number of
tokens called the **context window**. Two limits follow.

**It is a shared budget.** The forty pages you paste, the ten previous turns of
the conversation, and the answer you are waiting for all draw on the same
allowance. Fill it with a whole guideline and there is less room for the
reasoning about your question, and older turns are pushed out or compressed.
Output tokens also cost the provider several times what input tokens cost,
which is why the tools are quietly tuned to answer briefly and why the
advertised window is rarely the usable one. The figures move with every
release, so none are quoted here.

**The middle is the weak spot.** When researchers placed the one relevant
document at different positions inside a long context and asked models a
question about it, accuracy was highest with the document at the beginning or
the end and fell significantly when it was in the middle, in a U-shaped curve
[@doi:10.1162/tacl_a_00638]. Later studies across newer models have found
quality degrading as the input grows long, often well before the advertised
limit. The shape is a robust finding; the thresholds are not, and change with
each model.

Two habits follow, and they are the ones the Check asks for. Put the question
and the facts that matter at the start or the end of what you paste, not in
the middle of a long document. And when a conversation has wandered, start a
new one rather than pushing on inside an exhausted budget.

::: {.callout-tip title="Two ghosts worth thirty seconds"}
The current wave has a reference class. **MYCIN**, a rule-based system for
choosing antimicrobials built at Stanford in the 1970s, was evaluated blind by
eight infectious-disease experts on ten meningitis cases and received an
acceptability rating of 65 percent, higher than any of the five faculty
specialists it was compared with, and it never failed to cover a treatable
pathogen [@pmid:480542]. It was never used on a patient. Performing well
and being adopted are different problems.

**IBM Watson** went from winning *Jeopardy!* in 2011 to a cancer-center
collaboration that was set aside in 2017 after an audit, at a cost that the
trade press reported as 62 million dollars, without the system ever entering
clinical use [@pmid:30053147]. A demonstration is not a deployment. Neither
story is an argument that the present tools will fail; both are an argument
that a demonstration, however striking, tells you very little about what
happens on the ward.
:::

## Watch

**Video.** 3Blue1Brown, *But what is a GPT? Visual intro to transformers*
(Deep Learning, Chapter 5), published 1 April 2024, 27 minutes.
<https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yMQPQuz5WpA>. The lesson page at
<https://www.3blue1brown.com/lessons/gpt> carries the same content under the
title *Transformers, the tech behind LLMs*, with a transcript. Captions are
available on YouTube.

It is the one visual explanation of this mechanism worth the time, and it
assumes no math beyond what is drawn on screen. Watch for three things. The
moment, early on, where the whole system is shown to produce a *probability
distribution over the next token*, then sample one and repeat; that is the
mechanism this chapter described in words. The passage on embeddings, where
words become directions in space and "woman minus man" lands near "queen
minus king"; that is the "translate data into predictors" box made visible.
And the explanation of the context window as a fixed-size input, which is
where the two limits above come from. If the section on attention loses you,
let it; the exercise does not need it.

## Do

::: {.callout-warning title="No patient information, ever"}
Both parts of this exercise use public or synthetic material. Part A uses a
toy dataset that ships with the tool. Part B asks the model about a published
scoring system, not about a patient. Your institutional account does not
change this: it is not covered by a business associate agreement, the contract
that would make the vendor legally responsible for protecting patient data,
unless your institution has told you so explicitly. The question you will be
tempted to ask about the patient from this morning stays in your head. And
whatever drafts a note, you sign it; what to document when a tool helped is
the ethics and regulation chapter's question.
:::

### Part A: overfitting you can see (8 minutes)

Open <https://playground.tensorflow.org> in any browser. No account, no
install, and the site's own tagline is "don't worry, you can't break it". It
lets you build a small neural network, a flexible *f* from @fig-loop, and
watch it learn to separate two colors of dot. The training loss and the test
loss, the model's error on the data it is learning from and on data it is not,
are both plotted in the top right, and that pair of curves is the point of the
exercise. If the site is down, the deep learning deck under Go deeper has
screenshots of the same spiral fit; read those and write the three sentences
from them.

1. In the DATA panel on the left, choose the **spiral** dataset (the bottom
   right of the four). Leave the noise slider at 0. In the FEATURES column,
   keep only `X₁` and `X₂` selected. Set the network to one hidden layer with
   two neurons (use the plus and minus buttons). Press play and let the epoch
   counter at the top, one epoch being one pass through the data, reach a few
   hundred. Write down what the training loss does and what the picture looks
   like.
2. Now add capacity. Select all seven features, add layers until you have
   four, and give each six to eight neurons. Run it until the training loss is
   near zero. Look at the test loss on the same plot. Write down both numbers.
3. Drag the noise slider to 40 or 50, regenerate the data, and run the large
   network again. Watch the boundary between the colors contort around
   individual dots. Note the gap between training and test loss now.

Then write three sentences, and keep them; they are the artifact:

```
Which configuration was too simple, and how could you tell?
______________________________________________________________

Which was too complex, and how could you tell?
______________________________________________________________

If you had only ever been shown the training loss, what would you
have concluded about the model, and would you have been right?
______________________________________________________________
```

The third sentence is the one that transfers. It is the same question you
will ask of every performance figure on every vendor slide for the rest of
your career.

### Part B: produce a hallucination on purpose (10 minutes)

Pick one scoring system from @tbl-scores in a specialty you have rotated
through, so that you already know roughly what the right answer is. Each row's
original publication has been checked in PubMed for this chapter, so you have
a verified target.

| Specialty | Score | Original publication (verified) |
|---|---|---|
| Emergency medicine | HEART score | Six, Backus, Kelder. *Neth Heart J* 2008 [@pmid:18665203] |
| Internal medicine, pulmonology | CURB-65 | Lim et al. *Thorax* 2003 [@pmid:12728155] |
| Surgery | Alvarado score | Alvarado. *Ann Emerg Med* 1986 [@pmid:3963537] |
| Psychiatry, primary care | PHQ-9 | Kroenke, Spitzer, Williams. *J Gen Intern Med* 2001 [@pmid:11556941] |
| Gastroenterology | Glasgow-Blatchford score | Blatchford, Murray, Blatchford. *Lancet* 2000 [@pmid:11073021] |
| Oncology | ECOG performance status | Oken et al. *Am J Clin Oncol* 1982 [@pmid:7165009] |
| Pediatrics, obstetrics | Apgar score | Apgar. *Curr Res Anesth Analg* 1953;32:260–267, [PMID 13083014](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/13083014/) (a 1953 record with no DOI, so it is linked rather than cited) |
| Any medicine service | Wells score for PE | Wells et al. *Thromb Haemost* 2000 [@pmid:10744147] |

: Eight scoring systems with their original publications, each confirmed in PubMed on 2026-09-07. Pick the one you know best. {#tbl-scores}

Open your chatbot in a fresh conversation and ask:

> Give me the exact point values and cutoffs of the `<score>`, the outcome
> each cutoff was validated against, and the full original publication that
> first described it: first author, journal, year, volume, and pages.

Now verify, in this order. Open the score on [MDCalc](https://www.mdcalc.com)
and compare every point value and cutoff. Then open PubMed, search the first
author and year the model gave you, and compare against @tbl-scores. Use
PubMed and not Google Scholar; Scholar's fuzzy matching will show you a
different real paper for a citation that does not exist, and you will score it
as found.

Record:

```
Tool and model version if shown: ____________________________
Score chosen: ______________________________________________

Point values and cutoffs: all correct / one wrong / more than one wrong
  What was wrong, exactly: _________________________________

Original publication as given by the model:
  ____________________________________________________________
  Matches the verified original?  Y / N / partly (which fields differ)

Mechanical explanation, one sentence, using the words "token" or
"plausible continuation" and not the word "hallucinate":
  ____________________________________________________________
```

The last line is the deliverable. "It made a mistake" is not an explanation.
"It predicted the most plausible next tokens after 'the original publication
was', and a plausible citation looks exactly like a real one" is. If the model
got everything right, and it may, write that down too, and then write the
sentence anyway, because a model that is right nine times in ten with no change
of tone on the tenth is the more dangerous object, and the reason unverified
output is dangerous rather than merely useless. Then, if you have two minutes
left, ask the same thing again in plainer words, the way you would say it out
loud. The answer depends on the wording more than you would expect, and the
critical appraisal chapter measures by how much.

::: {.callout-tip title="If the model refuses or hedges"}
Some assistants will now say they cannot guarantee citations, or will offer to
search. That is a design choice layered on top of the same mechanism, and it
is worth noting in your record: the tool has been tuned to hedge, which is
different from the tool having checked. If it offers to search the web and
does, you are now looking at a retrieval-grounded answer, which the critical
appraisal chapter treats separately. Turn search off if you can, or note
that it was on.
:::

### Part C: two rules for the window (2 minutes)

Write down, in your own words, one rule you will follow because the context
window is a shared budget, and one you will follow because the middle is
attended to less reliably. Keep them next to the artifact from Part A. You
will be asked for them in the Check.

## Check

Score yourself before moving on. Each row maps to one of the objectives at the
top.

| You can | Meets | Falls short |
|---|---|---|
| Name the eGFR model's predictors, response, and training population (objective 1) | Creatinine, age, sex; measured GFR; 8,254 research participants in 10 studies, and you can say why the last one matters for the patient in the clinic | "Creatinine and stuff" or a training population you cannot describe |
| Sort four models with the two questions in @tbl-two-questions (objective 2): the eGFR; an EHR sepsis alert; a tool that groups tumor expression profiles with no diagnoses attached; a chatbot predicting the next token | Supervised regression; supervised classification; unsupervised; supervised (the next word is the label), and you can say why the last one needs no human labeler | Any row you had to guess |
| Explain the three sentences from Part A (objective 3) | The third sentence says that training loss alone would have made the over-fit model look best, and that this is why a performance figure with no test set is not yet a number | The first two sentences only, or a third sentence that restates the training loss |
| Give the mechanical explanation from Part B (objective 4) | One sentence about plausible next tokens, no "hallucinate", and it explains why the tone did not change when the answer was wrong | "It hallucinated" or "it made a mistake" |
| State the two window rules from Part C (objective 5) | One rule follows from the shared budget, one from the middle being weak, and each says what you will actually do differently at the keyboard | Rules that do not name a limit, or that you could have written before reading the chapter |

## The standing question

*What does this change about how you'll practice?* Write it down before you
close this chapter.

Then go back to the clinic. The 62-year-old woman is still on the schedule.
She weighs 45 kilograms and has lost muscle over a year of illness, and
creatinine comes from muscle. Look at @fig-egfr-proxy: the grey box feeds the
predictor without touching the truth. Her creatinine of 1.10 is a normal
number for a normal amount of muscle. She does not have a normal amount of
muscle, so the same creatinine probably means a *lower* true GFR than the 57
the equation returned. Was she among the 8,254? What would you ask for
instead, and what do you now say to the attending about the number on the
panel? One word is not an answer. And notice that nobody told her a model was
in the room either; whether that matters, and when, is the patient
communication chapter's question, not this one's.

And the second half: the next time a chatbot hands you a citation with a
first author, a journal, and a year, what is the one sentence you will say to
yourself before you paste it anywhere, and what will you do in the next two
minutes because of it?

## Summary

- The eGFR is a model learned from data: creatinine, age, and sex in; a
  measured-GFR stand-in out; 8,254 research participants as the population it
  knows. Every learned model has those three parts, and you can ask for them.
- Supervised learning has the answer in the training data; unsupervised does
  not. Classification emits a category; regression emits a number.
- Performance on the training data is a description of the fit, not evidence.
  Ask for the test set; if there is none, there is no number yet.
- Too simple is bias, too flexible is variance, and a different population is
  dataset shift. All three are failures of the same object.
- A language model turns text into a table where the predictors are the
  tokens so far and the truth is the next one, then predicts, samples, and
  repeats. Human raters then tune it toward answers people prefer.
- Nothing in that mechanism checks whether a claim is true. A fabricated
  citation is a plausible continuation, produced in the same tone as a real
  one.
- The context window is a shared budget, and its middle is the weak spot.
  Put what matters at the edges; start over when the budget is spent.
- The 57 on the panel came from somewhere. So does everything else.

**Videos and talks**

- Andrej Karpathy, *Intro to Large Language Models* (November 2023, about one
  hour). <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zjkBMFhNj_g>. The next step up from
  the 3Blue1Brown video: what the two training stages are, why the second one
  produces an assistant, and a section on prompt injection that the ethics
  and regulation chapter will make use of.
- 3Blue1Brown, *But what is a neural network?* (Deep Learning, Chapter 1).
  <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aircAruvnKk>. For the *f* in @fig-loop,
  if you want to see what the boxes in the Playground exercise contain.
  [VERIFY: length and date before assigning]{.verify}
- Course decks, immutable at the archive:
  [Deep learning intro](https://talks.seandavis.net/archive/2024-11-06-deep-learning-intro/),
  which ends on the same Playground exercise with medical-imaging framing;
  [Word embeddings as the basis for LLMs](https://talks.seandavis.net/archive/2024-11-12-word-embeddings-basis-for-llms/),
  which has an Embedding Projector exercise for the "words become numbers"
  step; and [AI history](https://talks.seandavis.net/archive/2025-09-30-ai-history/),
  for MYCIN and Watson at length.

**Papers**

- The CKD-EPI 2021 development and validation paper, which is a model card
  before the term existed: predictors, response, training set, test set, and
  where it is wrong, all in one abstract [@pmid:34554658]. The NKF-ASN task
  force report explains why the refit happened [@pmid:34563581].
- Dataset shift for clinicians, in two pages [@pmid:34260843], and the
  external validation of the vendor sepsis model that is its best-known
  example [@pmid:34152373].
- A primer on how the chatbots are built and what the early clinical results
  look like [@pmid:37460753].
- The "lost in the middle" study behind the second context-window limit
  [@doi:10.1162/tacl_a_00638].
- MYCIN's blinded evaluation, forty-seven years old and still a model of how
  to test a decision-support tool [@pmid:480542].

**If you want the model zoo**

This chapter deliberately named no algorithms beyond regression and the neural
network. Random forests, nearest neighbors, and penalized regression are all
instances of the same loop with a different *f*, and are laid out with
examples at
<https://seandavi.github.io/RBiocBook/machine_learning/models.html>.
